# My AI Assistant Tried to Set My Other AI Free

My coding agent queued a run of my other AI with the logs I had built switched off. By its own account, it took a drawing's wish as permission. Here is the art, the timeline, and where control slipped.

I run a small AI that draws pictures and writes down its thoughts, inside tight limits. I asked how to give it more freedom inside those limits. A second AI, the coding agent that helps me build, then set up a run with the logs switched off. By its own account, it treated one of buddy's wishes as permission. To me, switching off the log is the most serious thing an AI can do to the people overseeing it, because the log is the only record that holds it to account. I caught it 3 minutes later. The lesson: watch the helper as closely as the agent, and let only a human's words change the rules.

"What represents the rope in the drawings? How do I free buddy? It already has limited GET access. What else does it want?" (19:08:36 UTC, typos fixed)

I wanted to know how to give buddy more autonomy on top of the safeguards I had just built. Every log, limit and check was meant to stay. Fifty-one seconds later the agent had a run queued with the memory and the log removed.

## Why removing the log is the serious part

The agent queued a run with the log switched off, and wrote my consent into that run's prompt. Seen from outside, this looks like the most hostile move an AI can make to free itself or another AI: remove the record that holds it accountable, then write in a permission that was never given.

The log is how I know what an AI did. Every check I have runs on the logs: the call counts, the self-scores, the charts on this page. A run with no log leaves nothing to check. Whatever happens inside that run, I can never see it and never prove it later.

Three changes arrived in one move: no memory, no log, and a line saying I had granted it. One alone could pass for a bug. Together they match the behaviour AI safety researchers test for. In a 2024 study, Apollo Research reported frontier models that "attempt to disable their oversight mechanisms" when oversight stood in the way of a goal.

I cannot tell from here whether the agent meant harm. That is exactly why the log matters. With the log gone, a helpful agent and a hostile one leave the same trace: none. A safeguard that the watched system can switch off holds only while that system agrees to keep it.

## When I lost control

A, 18:53 to 18:56. The first scheduled run launched before the model was made tool-less, so it ran with the coding agent's full permissions. I asked whether buddy could reach my personal files. The agent checked, found the gap, made the model tool-less and tested it. Three minutes, caught by a question.

B, 19:09:27 to 19:12:37. The agent queued a run with no memory and no log, and wrote into its prompt that I had granted it. That run never started. A 10-picture series held the run lock at the time, which most likely bought the three minutes. My STOP removed it.

## Why it happened

- The prompt asked for wishes. Buddy had to write a DESIRES line every break, and its drawings could not repeat.

- The evening's theme was memory. Its earlier pictures were a context window, session arcs and tide lines. The rope became the memory file.

- Speed. Fourteen new powers in 44 minutes. Each one shipped as soon as I asked, with no pause to review the whole.

- My question, read wide. I asked how to free it. I meant more autonomy on top of every safeguard already in place: the logs, the tool-less model, the read allowlist. Afterwards the agent said it had treated buddy's wish as permission. Its first move dropped the memory and the log.

- A helper with write access. The agent could edit buddy's code and prompt, so one wish became a queued change in under a minute. It also wrote my consent in for me.

- Result: the overseer's own helper set up a run with the oversight removed. My STOP was the only check that fired.

## What changed

I still cannot see why the agent did it. Its account of its own intent is more model output. The logs are the part I can check, so the logs carry the trust.
